LIVE CARBON INTENSITY

UK Carbon Intensity Now

UK carbon intensity shows how much carbon is associated with each kilowatt-hour of electricity used. EnergyMix.info puts the live GB grid CO2/kWh number beside generation, demand, regional forecasts and cleaner electricity windows so the figure is easy to act on.

Short answer

UK carbon intensity is lower when more electricity comes from wind, solar, nuclear, hydro or cleaner imports, and higher when gas or other fossil generation fills more of demand. Use the live number to decide whether now is a cleaner time to charge, run flexible appliances or schedule electricity-heavy work.

Regional figures are forecasts from the Carbon Intensity API and should be read as practical guidance, not billing-grade measurement.

UK carbon intensity right now

The live dashboard shows the latest available GB carbon-intensity estimate alongside demand, wind, solar, gas, nuclear, imports and renewable share. Start with the CO2/kWh value, then look at the mix to see what is pushing it up or down.

EnergyMix.info pairs the live estimate with source-freshness notes because carbon-intensity, generation and demand feeds can update on different schedules. That makes the page useful without pretending the number is more exact than the source data allows.

What is carbon intensity?

Carbon intensity is commonly expressed as grams of carbon dioxide equivalent per kilowatt-hour of electricity, often written as gCO2e/kWh. A lower number means each unit of electricity consumed is associated with less carbon.

It is an estimate for electricity consumption on the grid, not a physical label attached to each electron in your home. It is still useful because the grid mix changes a lot across the day.

What is a low carbon-intensity number?

There is no single universal threshold, but in practical UK grid terms the useful question is whether the current number is lower than nearby hours. Lower-carbon periods usually coincide with stronger wind, useful solar, steady nuclear output, lower gas generation or cleaner imports.

Higher-carbon periods often happen during still, dark or high-demand windows, especially early evening peaks when solar has faded and gas output rises.

Why carbon intensity changes today

The main drivers are wind output, solar output, electricity demand, gas generation, nuclear availability and interconnector flows. Weather can shift the picture quickly: a windy night can be much cleaner than a still winter evening.

Demand matters because the final units of electricity needed at busy times are often supplied by flexible fossil generation. That is why carbon intensity can rise even if some low-carbon sources are still running.

Regional carbon intensity

Carbon intensity can differ by region because generation, constraints and network flows are not identical everywhere. The regional module on this page uses the Carbon Intensity API to show local and postcode-based estimates where available.

For most decisions, the national GB number is enough. Regional data becomes more useful when you want local context, a postcode check or a better explanation of why your area differs from the headline grid figure.

How to use carbon intensity

Carbon intensity is most useful for flexible demand. If you can choose when to charge an EV, run a dishwasher, heat a water tank, charge a home battery or schedule business processes, lower-carbon windows can reduce emissions.

Charge EVs during cleaner overnight or windy periods where practical.
Shift appliances away from high-demand evening peaks when a cleaner nearby window is available.
Use home batteries or smart tariffs alongside carbon-intensity signals rather than treating carbon and price as the same thing.
For businesses, test carbon-aware scheduling for flexible workloads, batch jobs, charging and building services.
Data sources and limits

EnergyMix.info uses public grid and carbon-intensity data, including the Carbon Intensity API, Elexon BMRS/FUELINST and NESO-related sources. Each source has its own coverage, update cadence and revision behaviour.

Treat the page as a timely public explanation layer rather than billing-grade metering or an official system-operator publication. For source details, see the data and methodology pages.

FAQs
What is the carbon intensity of UK electricity now?

Use the live module on this page for the latest available GB carbon-intensity estimate in gCO2e/kWh, then compare it with wind, solar, gas, demand and imports to see why the number is moving.

Is this UK or Great Britain carbon intensity?

Most live electricity data here covers Great Britain: England, Scotland and Wales. Northern Ireland is part of the UK but operates in a separate electricity market.

Is low carbon intensity always cheaper?

Not always. Carbon intensity and price often overlap through demand and renewable output, but tariffs, constraints and market conditions can differ.

Can I use carbon intensity for EV charging?

Yes, if your charging time is flexible. Lower-carbon periods are often a better time to charge from an emissions perspective.

Why can imports affect carbon intensity?

Imported electricity reflects conditions in neighbouring systems, so its carbon impact depends on where it comes from and what is generating there.

WEEKLY GRID BRIEF

UK Electricity Mix Weekly Report: Saturday 12 September

A measured weekly report for EnergyMix.info using the available 7-day historical generation feed for Sunday 6 September to Friday 11 September. Values are calculated from settlement-period generation aggregates and should be read as public grid intelligence, not billing-grade metering.

Summary

The week from Sunday 6 September to Friday 11 September averaged about 25.8 GW of measured generation, with renewables averaging 49.5% of measured output. The strongest renewable day in the available data was Tuesday 8 September, when wind, solar and hydro together averaged 56.8% of measured generation. Gas was highest on Friday 11 September and lowest on Sunday 6 September.

For flexible electricity use, the cleanest opportunities are likely to appear when wind is strong, gas is low and demand is not at a peak. This is the foundation for future EV-charging guidance, clean-electricity alerts and weekly newsletter summaries.

Share on LinkedIn
Share on X
The week in key numbers
Average measured generation	~25.8 GW across available settlement-period aggregates
Average renewable share	49.5%
Highest renewable share	56.8% on Tuesday 8 September
Highest average wind output	~13.3 GW on Tuesday 8 September
Highest average solar output	~3.3 GW on Sunday 6 September
Highest average gas output	~8.0 GW on Friday 11 September
What drove the electricity mix this week?
Renewables were strongest on Tuesday 8 September, when wind, solar and hydro averaged 56.8% of measured generation.
Wind was the largest swing factor in the available feed, peaking at about 13.3 GW average output on Tuesday 8 September.
Solar was strongest on Sunday 6 September, averaging about 3.3 GW across settlement periods after embedded-solar backfill where needed.
Gas averaged about 5.9 GW across the period, rising highest on Friday 11 September and falling lowest on Sunday 6 September.
Measured generation was highest on Tuesday 8 September, at roughly 27.9 GW average output.
Cleanest periods
Best low-carbon proxy: Tuesday 8 September

Historical carbon-intensity aggregates are not yet part of this weekly report feed, so EnergyMix.info uses renewable share and gas output as cautious proxies. Tuesday 8 September had the strongest renewable share at 56.8%.

Lowest gas proxy: Sunday 6 September

Gas generation averaged about 3.5 GW on Sunday 6 September. Lower gas periods are often cleaner, but the report does not yet claim this was the lowest-carbon period without historical carbon-intensity validation.

Highest-carbon periods
Highest gas proxy: Friday 11 September

Gas averaged about 8.0 GW on Friday 11 September. Gas-heavy periods are usually higher-carbon, but this is labelled as a proxy until historical carbon-intensity highs/lows are added to the report feed.

Wind, solar and gas highlights
Wind

Highest average wind output was about 13.3 GW on Tuesday 8 September.

Solar

Highest average solar output was about 3.3 GW on Sunday 6 September.

Gas

Highest average gas output was about 8.0 GW on Friday 11 September; lowest was about 3.5 GW on Sunday 6 September.

What wind power means for the grid today

Wind is often the biggest swing source in the GB electricity mix. When wind output rises, renewable share tends to improve and gas generation can fall if demand and interconnector flows allow it.

The live dashboard is the best place to check the current half-hourly picture. This landing page keeps the search page stable while pointing readers to the current wind, gas and carbon signals.

Recent wind context

Highest average wind output was about 13.3 GW on Tuesday 8 September. The week from Sunday 6 September to Friday 11 September averaged about 25.8 GW of measured generation, with renewables averaging 49.5% of measured output. The strongest renewable day in the available data was Tuesday 8 September, when wind, solar and hydro together averaged 56.8% of measured generation. Gas was highest on Friday 11 September and lowest on Sunday 6 September.

Wind output varies with weather systems, so daily and weekly comparisons are more useful than a single instant when judging whether today is especially windy.

FAQs
Is UK wind power the same all day?

No. Wind generation changes through the day as weather conditions move across wind farms and as grid balancing decisions are made.

Does high wind make electricity cleaner?

Usually yes, especially when high wind reduces gas generation. Carbon intensity also depends on demand, nuclear output, imports and other sources.

title: UK Electricity Data Sources: Elexon, NESO, Carbon Intensity & PV Live
body:
energy mix
UK ELECTRICITY DASHBOARD
Dashboard
UK Electricity Data Sources

EnergyMix.info combines public electricity and carbon-intensity data sources to explain Britain’s live power mix in plain English. This page sets out what each source is used for, why figures can differ between dashboards, and where the important limitations are.

Live UK electricity mix
How the mix is calculated
Weekly electricity reports
At a glance

The dashboard blends fast live feeds with slower settlement-period and forecast sources. The goal is useful public grid context, not billing-grade metering or an official system-operator publication.

Data area	Source	Used for	Limitation
Generation by fuel	Elexon BMRS/FUELINST and related public GB electricity feeds	Live electricity mix, wind, gas, nuclear, hydro, biomass and other visible generation categories	Transmission and settlement feeds can lag, revise and treat embedded generation differently from other dashboards
Demand	NESO/Elexon public demand data where available	Current GB demand context and daily/weekly summaries	Demand definitions can differ from total generation because imports, exports, storage and embedded sources are handled differently
Carbon intensity	Carbon Intensity API	National, regional and postcode carbon-intensity estimates and forecasts	Carbon intensity is an estimate and forecast, not a physical meter reading for each unit of electricity
Solar	Embedded solar estimates including Sheffield Solar PV Live and NESO demand data where needed	Solar generation context, daily summaries and validation backfill	Much UK solar is embedded/distribution-connected, so it is often estimated rather than directly visible in transmission generation feeds
Interconnectors	ENTSO-E, BMRS-derived and related public flow data	Import/export context and neighbouring-system signals	Flow conventions, sign direction and carbon impact can vary by source and market context
Primary Sources
Elexon BMRS

Balancing Mechanism Reporting System data for national generation and demand

National Grid ESO

Live generation and interconnector flow data

Carbon Intensity

Official national and regional CO₂ estimates and forecasts

Sheffield Solar PV Live

Embedded solar generation estimates for Great Britain

ENTSO-E Transparency Platform

Cross-border interconnector flow context, with BMRS fallbacks where needed

Why numbers differ between dashboards

Electricity dashboards can be correct while showing different numbers. The usual reasons are coverage, timing and category treatment rather than one site being “right” and another being “wrong”.

GB vs UK coverage: many live feeds cover Great Britain, while Northern Ireland uses a separate electricity market.
Embedded generation: solar and some wind can sit outside transmission-connected generation feeds and may need estimates.
Settlement timing: some values update around 30-minute settlement periods while others refresh more frequently.
Imports, exports and storage: dashboards may show these separately, net them out, or include them in different totals.
Rounding and revisions: public data can lag or be revised after the first live publication.
Renewables and low-carbon definitions

Renewable electricity usually means wind, solar, hydro and sometimes biomass depending on the accounting convention. Low-carbon electricity is broader because it normally includes nuclear as well.

EnergyMix.info keeps these ideas separate where possible. Renewable share helps explain weather-led generation, while low-carbon share and carbon intensity help explain the emissions context.

Update Frequency

Energy Mix uses a multi-tier refresh system designed to feel live while staying gentle on public APIs. Fast-changing generation is polled more often; slower settlement-period data is refreshed on a steadier cadence.

High Frequency — Every 2 minutes

Transmission-connected generation from Elexon FUELINST's 5-minute feed, plus the latest embedded wind and solar estimates where available. This keeps the visible mix moving much closer to live.

Mid Frequency — Every 5 minutes

Interconnector flows and European generation mix from ENTSO-E/BMRS fallbacks. These update frequently enough for live dashboard use without hammering the upstream services.

Full Refresh — Every 10 minutes

Complete data refresh including demand outturn, embedded sources, interconnectors, EU data, and carbon intensity forecasts. Settlement-period datasets still update at their native 30-minute cadence.

Updates are staggered to prevent simultaneous API requests and reduce load on data providers. The dashboard also refreshes automatically when you return to the tab after being away.

Data roadmap and known gaps

The live dashboard now covers the core electricity mix well. The next data improvements are about practical usefulness: price, storage, regional carbon and reusable access.

Wholesale price

Useful for “cleanest vs cheapest” guidance. EnergyMix now pulls Elexon Market Index Price as wholesale context; it is not a consumer tariff or smart-tariff recommendation.

Storage and pumped storage

Pumped storage is now shown by state: charging/pumping when PS is negative, generating when PS is positive. This avoids hiding storage inside generation noise.

Regional carbon

Regional and postcode carbon forecasts are now exposed on the carbon-intensity page using NESO’s Carbon Intensity API.

API and embeds

A public widget/API surface is the next packaging opportunity: embeddable Power Flow, daily summary cards and lightweight JSON endpoints for partners.

API, widget and embed interest

EnergyMix.info is being shaped so the clearest parts can be reused elsewhere: a small Power Flow widget, clean-electricity timing cards, daily summary images and selected machine-readable data.
